core: market research as decision-focused collection and interpretation of market evidence
research questions, populations, samples, and evidence limits
ethical participation and careful handling of personal information
supporting: official demographic and economic data tools
industry classification as a way to locate relevant official business statistics
qualitative and quantitative evidence as different but complementary forms of evidence
outOfScope: customer-interview recruiting, prompts, moderation, and note-taking mechanics
individualized business, legal, tax, financial, investment, or fundraising advice
claiming that research proves market demand, a revenue forecast, or venture success

claims.claim: Market research collects and analyzes information about a target market so an organization can answer decision-relevant questions about customers and market conditions.
Primary research creates new data for a defined question, while secondary research uses data already collected by another entity; they answer different kinds of questions and can be combined.

Official Census tools can supply selected demographic and economic information by location and business type, while NAICS is the federal standard for classifying business establishments for U.S. business statistics.

A sample supports claims only about the population, sampling frame, and method that justify them; larger samples can reduce sampling error but do not by themselves fix coverage, selection, response, measurement, or interpretation problems.

Research involving people should respect voluntary participation, avoid misleading participants, explain the use of identifiable information, limit access to identifiers, and avoid collecting or retaining sensitive personal information without a legitimate need.
Uncertainty should be reported with the estimate, method, relevant population, and limitations; a margin of error describes sampling uncertainty for a sample estimate rather than all possible error.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a larger sample alone makes market-research findings representative.
positions: Larger samples generally reduce sampling error for a properly defined sample estimate.
A large convenience sample can still omit important people or contain systematic response and measurement bias.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes sampling uncertainty from coverage, selection, response, and measurement limits; it does not promise representativeness from sample size alone.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic statements and did not provide an evidence-supported definition, method distinction, sample limit, or ethical handling guidance.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with a decision-focused definition of market research.
Added the distinction between new primary data and existing secondary data.
Added population, sampling-frame, sample, uncertainty, and generalizability limits.
Added bounded ethical guidance for voluntary participation and responsible personal-data handling.
Removed any implication that market research proves demand, a forecast, or business success.
rightsIssues: SBA, Census, FTC, and AAPOR sources are used as reference-only authoritative guidance; no source prose was adapted.
OpenStax states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with attribution, but this lesson is original synthesis and does not reproduce source prose.

sourceRecords.title: Market research and competitive analysis
sourceRecords.notes: Official small-business guidance. Supports market-research questions, the distinction between existing and direct research, and the limits of broad existing data for a specific audience. The original URL was read and redirected by SBA to its current planning page.

sourceRecords.title: 8.2 Market Research, Market Opportunity Recognition, and Target Market
sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook chapter defining primary and secondary market research and describing research goals, designs, samples, data collection, and limits. Used for original synthesis only; the page says separate permission is needed for AI training or ingestion.

sourceRecords.title: Census Business Builder (CBB)
sourceRecords.notes: Official description of the current Census Business Builder service, including selected demographic and economic data, location and business-type selection, maps, dashboards, and downloadable reports.

sourceRecords.title: North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)
sourceRecords.notes: Official explanation that federal statistical agencies use NAICS to classify U.S. business establishments for collecting, analyzing, and publishing business-economy statistics.

sourceRecords.title: Sample Size Definitions
sourceRecords.notes: Official guidance explaining that sample-based estimates have sampling uncertainty, that larger samples generally have less sampling error, and that published ACS margins of error express 90-percent confidence intervals. Used to explain the bounded meaning of sampling uncertainty.

sourceRecords.title: AAPOR Code of Professional Ethics and Practices
sourceRecords.provider: American Association for Public Opinion Research
sourceRecords.notes: Current professional ethics code (revised June 2026) supporting voluntary participation, truthful purpose disclosure, privacy protection, appropriate method choice, accurate reporting, and limits on generalizing from samples.

sourceRecords.title: Protecting Personal Information: A Guide for Business
sourceRecords.notes: Official practical guidance supporting data minimization, legitimate retention periods, restricted access, secure storage, and disposal of sensitive personal information. This is not presented as a complete statement of jurisdiction-specific law.
